E045-01.notes: ', and they wanted' correctly joins two independent clauses (comma + coordinating conjunction). B: comma splice ('...in Europe, they wanted a lighter version'). C: 'and, they wanted' puts a needless comma after the conjunction. D: 'and they, wanted' splits subject from verb. All four substitutions read cleanly as to spacing; only A is grammatical.

E045-02.notes: Nonessential 'whose' clause needs a comma before it, matching the comma after 'aluminum'. B drops the opening comma, so the clause is set off on one side only. C: a semicolon before a dependent relative clause leaves fragments. D: 'Dalquist, his small company, Nordic Ware, made...' makes 'his small company' an appositive renaming Dalquist, which is illogical, and it leaves 'made' and 'agreed' without a proper structure.

E045-03.notes: Conciseness. B 'made it possible for heat to be able to reach' is doubly redundant. C 'let heat be able to reach' repeats the idea of 'let'. D 'allowed and permitted' uses two synonyms.

E045-04.notes: The adverb 'poorly' modifies the verb 'sold'. A uses the adjective 'poor'. C and D are comparative adjectives, and nothing is being compared.

E045-05.notes: A trivia sentence about aluminum's abundance and other uses is off topic in a paragraph about designing and naming the pan. A is wrong: the sentence gives no reason for the material choice. B misreads the sentence's purpose. D is wrong: the sentence contradicts nothing. Fact check: aluminum is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust (oxygen and silicon are more abundant, but they are not metals), so the sentence is accurate.

E045-06.notes: Sentence 7 gives a cause of the poor sales in sentence 6, and 'One reason was that' signals exactly that. B 'As a result' reverses the cause and effect. C 'However' and D 'Even so' signal a contrast that is not there.

flags.note: B is a tempting distractor because it names Helfrich, but it is still a dangling modifier: Helfrich was not baked in the pan.

E045-07.notes: The modifier 'Baked in a Bundt pan' must attach to the cake. D does this. 'her' refers clearly to Helfrich in sentence 8. A: the ring of fudge was not baked in the pan. B: Helfrich was not baked. C: 'there' cannot be the thing baked, and the sentence is wordy.

E045-08.notes: One contest (the Bake-Off) owns the entry, so the singular possessive 'contest's' is needed. A has no apostrophe. B is a plural possessive. D 'the contest best-known entry' is ungrammatical.

E045-09.notes: The subject is the singular 'flood', and 'of requests from bakers who wanted...' is an intervening phrase, so the verb is 'was'. A and C are plural. C and D also clash with the past-tense narrative ('had to expand').

E045-10.notes: The essay traces years of poor sales, then the 1966 Bake-Off entry, then a surge in demand that forced Nordic Ware to expand. That matches the goal. A gives a design detail that is not the reason. C misstates the focus. D is factually false: sentence 10 says the cake won second place.
